content: What are the main business goals and real-world uses of the university publications repository in your institution?

The main goal is to keep a reliable central record of all VUB publications, both for internal reporting and for making research outputs easier to find and reuse. In practice, it is used by researchers and staff to deposit publication texts and metadata, by librarians or administrators to clean up and validate records, and by the university to support visibility, compliance, and performance reporting. It also helps us avoid duplicate records and handle cases where the same author or institution appears under different names.
How dependable does the repository need to be in day-to-day use, and what kinds of service interruptions or slowdowns would be acceptable or not acceptable for your users?

It needs to be dependable enough that staff can use it every day without worrying about losing records or uploads. Short slowdowns might be tolerable during busy periods, but we would not accept repeated outages or anything that risks corrupting publication data or blocking access for a whole working day. Search and download should stay reasonably responsive, because those are the functions people rely on most.

Could you walk me through what kinds of bibliographic information and publication files the repository needs to store for each record, and how you expect those pieces to relate to one another in day-to-day use?

For each record we need the basic bibliographic metadata like title, authors, affiliations, publication date, journal or conference details, DOI or other identifiers, and the publication type. We also need to store the actual full text files when they are available, and those files should be linked clearly to the right bibliographic record, because people need to see both the metadata and the document together. In day-to-day use, one publication may have several related files, like a submitted version and a final version, so the system should keep those relationships clear rather than treating everything as separate unrelated entries.

When you think about migrating your existing publication records and documents into the new repository, how would you describe the overall process you need, including what has to come across, what needs to stay linked together, and any important conditions or exceptions that shape how the migration should work?

We would need the migration to bring over the bibliographic metadata, the publication files, and any links between them so each record still points to the right document after import. It is also important to preserve relationships like authorship, institutional affiliation, and any existing identifiers or grouping that help us recognize the same publication across systems. Some older records may be incomplete or inconsistent, so those should still come across if possible, but flagged for later cleanup rather than blocking the whole migration.
Which legacy source repositories or data sets do you need to migrate into the new system?

I don’t have the exact list in front of me, so I’d need to verify that with the library or IT team. I do know there are existing publication data sets and document repositories we want to consolidate, but the specific source systems are something I shouldn’t guess on.

As you think about releasing and maintaining the new repository over time, what are the main business situations or operational goals that should shape how often it changes, how safely updates happen, and how easy it needs to be for your team to support it day to day?

We want changes to be managed carefully because the repository supports ongoing research reporting and document access, so updates should not disrupt normal use. Ideally, we would release improvements in a controlled way, with enough testing and rollback protection that staff can trust each update. Day to day, the system should also be easy for our team to support, meaning routine corrections, imports, and moderation should not require technical intervention every time.
Looking ahead, are there any planned enhancements or integrations you expect the repository to support, and if so, what conditions or constraints should guide how those are introduced over time?

Yes, we expect there will be future enhancements, especially around better search, metadata enrichment, and tighter integration with other university systems or external publication sources. Those should be added in a way that does not break existing records or workflows, and they need to respect our access rights and data quality rules. We would also want new integrations to be introduced gradually so we can validate them before they affect the whole repository.

Are there any specific phases of the publication lifecycle, such as initial deposit, later correction, versioning, or eventual archival or removal, where the repository’s purpose changes or where different operational rules should apply?

Yes, those phases do matter. Initial deposit should be straightforward and accept incomplete records if needed, while later correction and moderation should allow staff to refine or approve the metadata before it becomes final. Versioning is important because we may keep multiple stages of a publication, and archival should preserve the record long term even if the file is no longer actively edited; removal would only be for exceptional cases, like a duplicate or something that should not have been published there.
Would you like to add any other business goals or operational purposes for the repository now, or should we leave that part as tentative for the moment?

I think we should leave that part tentative for the moment. The main goals are clear enough for now, and I’d rather not overdefine additional business purposes until we’ve confirmed the core workflows and stakeholder needs.

Are there any specific conditions or exceptions under which a publication should move between deposit, correction, versioning, archival, or removal, such as handling duplicates, retractions, or records that were entered in error?

Yes, duplicates and records entered in error are the main cases where we would move or adjust a publication’s status. If a publication is retracted, we would want to keep the record but clearly mark it so it is no longer treated as current, while a duplicate might need to be merged or removed depending on whether it contains useful unique information. For accidental deposits, we would usually correct or delete them if they never should have been in the repository in the first place.

When a publication record is created or updated, what is the expected workflow for making those changes—who can enter the record, who can edit or approve it, and when does it become the authoritative version?

A normal expectation would be that researchers or delegated staff can enter or update records, but only authorized library or repository staff can approve and finalize them. Until approval, the record should still be treated as a draft or pending version, not the authoritative one. Once it has been reviewed and approved, that becomes the version everyone else relies on.

When an initial deposit is incomplete, what minimum information or materials do you need in order to accept it, and are there any cases where you would reject or hold it back until more details are provided?

At minimum, we would need enough information to identify the publication clearly, usually a title and some basic author or source details, plus the full text if that is available. If the record is too vague to distinguish it from others, or if the file appears to be the wrong item entirely, we would hold it back rather than accept it as-is. In some cases we might still accept it provisionally, but only if we can reasonably expect the missing details to be filled in later.
Who is allowed to propose a correction to a publication record, and does that differ depending on whether the record is still pending, already approved, or later found to be inaccurate?

Yes, it can differ. For pending records, the person who submitted it or repository staff can usually propose changes more freely, but once it is approved we would want corrections to come from authorized staff or from the original contributor if they have the proper role. If a record is later found to be inaccurate, we would expect repository staff to be able to intervene directly, because that is when it becomes a data quality issue rather than a normal edit.
What events, besides document upload and bulk import, can trigger the creation of a new publication record in the repository?

A manual entry by a researcher or staff member would be one, especially when a publication is known but no file is available yet. Another trigger could be metadata reconciliation from an external source, where we import a citation record first and attach the full text later if it becomes available. I’m not aware of other major triggers beyond that, but we may discover more during process mapping.

What should happen if the repository is unavailable or very slow during staff use—for example, is there a maximum acceptable outage or recovery time before search and retrieval are considered unusable?

We would definitely need the repository to be available during working hours, especially for library and repository staff who are processing deposits and corrections. I don’t have a precise maximum outage or recovery time in mind, but if search or retrieval is down long enough to block day-to-day work, that would be unacceptable. In practice, we would want interruptions to be rare and short, and there should be a clear way to resume work once the system comes back.
When you introduce a new integration, what rollout steps, pilot group, or fallback process should be used to validate it before it is allowed to affect the full repository?

We would normally want to test any new integration with a small pilot group first, probably repository staff only, before exposing it to all users or letting it write into the main repository data. During that pilot, we’d keep a fallback path so changes can be reverted or handled manually if something behaves unexpectedly. Once the results look stable and the data quality is acceptable, then it can be opened up more broadly.
When staff browse publication records, are there any specific rules for sorting, filtering, or default ordering that should apply, such as different behavior for certain record types or user roles?

By default, staff would probably want the most recent or most recently updated records first, because that is usually what they need to work on. Filters should at least support things like status, publication type, author, year, and whether the record has been approved or still needs review. I’m not aware of any special sorting rules by role, but some roles may need to see their own pending items more prominently.

For staff users who need to work on their own pending items, should the default sort or filter behavior give those records any extra prominence, and if so what rule should determine when that happens?

Yes, for staff who are actively processing items, their own pending records should probably be surfaced first by default. The simple rule would be to prioritize items assigned to them or items they created that are still pending, and then fall back to the normal recency sort. That way they can get back to unfinished work quickly without losing the general ordering for everything else.

When a publication record is still in draft or pending status before approval, who should be able to view, edit, or download it, and are there any restrictions on exposing the attached files at that stage?

While a record is still draft or pending, it should be limited to the contributor, repository staff, and moderators with the right access. Editing should be restricted to the people responsible for that record, and downloading the attached files should also be limited, because we do not want unfinished or unapproved material exposed broadly. If there is a file attached, I’d expect it to stay internal until the record is approved or explicitly cleared for access.

For actions like viewing, editing, or downloading records and files that are still protected, what audit details or review trail do you need to capture, and are there any actions that must be logged differently or not logged at all?

We should log who did what, when they did it, and which record or file was involved, especially for protected items. For edits, it would be useful to keep the before and after state or at least a version history so reviewers can see what changed. I don’t think there are actions that should not be logged at all, but some routine reads may only need basic access logging rather than a very detailed trail.

If an attached file is still internal while the record is draft or pending, are there any situations where someone should still be allowed to view, copy, or share it before approval, and if so who and under what conditions?

Yes, but only in very controlled cases. I’d expect repository staff and designated moderators to be able to view it for validation, and perhaps the original contributor if they need to correct or replace the file, but not copy or share it outside the process. If there is a temporary need to circulate it, that should be exceptional and tied to a specific review purpose, not a normal workflow.

What specific response time or availability expectations should we set for uploads, downloads, and full-text access during normal use and busy periods, and what should happen if the service becomes too slow or temporarily unavailable?

I’d expect normal browsing and metadata searches to stay responsive, but I don’t have exact seconds in mind yet and would need to confirm with the team. Uploads and downloads should complete reliably even during busy periods, though full-text access can take a bit longer as long as it does not feel broken to the user. If the service becomes too slow or unavailable, we should show a clear message, prevent duplicate submissions, and let users retry later rather than losing their work.

When the service is too slow or unavailable, what should the user experience be for an in-progress upload or download—for example, should they see a retry option, an error that preserves progress, or any point at which the system should automatically abandon the attempt?

For uploads, the user should definitely get a clear error that preserves whatever progress is possible, and a retry option if the transfer can be resumed. We should avoid automatically abandoning the attempt too quickly, because large publication files can take time and users would be frustrated if they have to start over. For downloads, a retry is fine, but if it cannot continue cleanly then the user should just be told it failed and can try again later.

For routine corrections, imports, and moderation, what specific steps or permissions should staff have so they can resolve most day-to-day issues themselves, and in which situations would technical support still need to step in?

Staff should be able to correct metadata, merge duplicate author or institution names, approve or reject pending records, and run or re-run bulk imports without needing technical help for every case. They should also be able to fix common problems like missing fields, wrong classifications, or attaching the right full text, as long as it stays within their role. Technical support would only need to step in for system errors, failed integrations, import format problems that the staff cannot interpret, or cases where a workflow is blocked by something outside the normal publication process.

For staff who can correct and moderate records themselves, what limits should apply to the changes they make—for example, which fields or record states can they edit, when would a second review or approval be required, and what should happen if they encounter a conflict they cannot resolve?

They should be able to edit the normal bibliographic fields and moderate records that are still in draft, pending, or otherwise not yet finalized. Once a record is approved or published, changes to key fields or the attached full text should probably require a second review, especially if it affects the public record or anything used for reporting. If they hit a conflict they can’t resolve, the system should let them flag it for another moderator or escalate it to a higher authority rather than forcing a guess.

When your team extracts bibliographic details from a document, what does the normal review and validation flow look like in your organization, and where do you need the system to step in when the extraction is incomplete, ambiguous, or conflicts with an existing record?

Normally, the system should prefill the fields from the document and then let a staff member check and correct them before the record is finalized. If the extraction is incomplete or ambiguous, I’d expect it to clearly mark the uncertain parts so the reviewer knows what still needs attention. When it conflicts with an existing record, the system should help compare them side by side and flag the possible duplicate or mismatch, but the final decision should stay with the moderator.
Which bibliographic fields should the system extract from an uploaded document beyond the basic bibliographic details?

Besides the basic title, authors, journal or venue, year, and DOI if present, it should try to capture things like abstract, keywords, volume, issue, pages, publisher, language, and affiliation information when it can find them. If the document contains references or funding acknowledgements, those could be useful too, but I’d treat those as secondary. The important thing is that the system should show what it extracted and let staff verify it rather than assuming it is always correct.

When extraction finds a possible duplicate or mismatch with an existing publication record, what should the moderator be able to compare side by side, and are there any conditions where the system should automatically treat it as a duplicate, leave it unresolved, or route it for escalation?

The moderator should be able to compare the title, authors, DOI, year, venue, and any attached full text side by side, along with whichever fields the system thinks are uncertain. If the DOI matches exactly, that would be a strong signal to treat it as the same publication, but I still think the moderator should confirm before merging. If the evidence is weak or conflicting, it should stay unresolved and be routed to a more experienced reviewer or escalated for manual checking.
What acceptable search response time should users expect before the system is considered too slow?

For normal searches, it should feel essentially immediate, ideally within a couple of seconds. If it takes longer than about five seconds, users will start to experience it as slow, and beyond that we should show that the system is still working rather than leaving them wondering.
Are there any additional bibliographic fields you want extracted only when they appear in a certain kind of document or source, or should the system always attempt all of them whenever possible?

I’d prefer the system always attempts the common fields whenever possible, but only extracts the more specialized ones when they are clearly present in that type of document. For example, conference papers and theses may have extra details that journal articles usually do not, so it should adapt to the source rather than forcing the same set every time. That way we get useful data without creating too much noise from false extractions.

When older records are migrated despite missing or inconsistent metadata, what specific cleanup flags, review statuses, or exception handling should the system apply so teams can identify and prioritize those records afterward?

Those records should come in with a clear migration flag and a review status like incomplete, uncertain, or needs validation, depending on what’s missing. If the inconsistency is serious, I’d want the system to keep the record searchable but visibly marked so staff can prioritize it later instead of losing it in the normal flow. Any fields imported from a questionable source should be traceable back to that source, so the team can decide whether to trust them or replace them.

When the system finds duplicate records with weak or conflicting evidence, what should determine whether it stays unresolved for later review versus being escalated immediately to a more experienced reviewer or manual checker?

I’d base that on the level of uncertainty and the impact of the record. If it’s just a low-confidence match and nothing critical is affected, it can stay unresolved in a review queue for later. But if the record is high priority, has conflicting identifiers, or there’s a risk of merging the wrong publication or author, then it should be escalated immediately to a more experienced reviewer.

When a migrated record is flagged as incomplete or uncertain, what should the system do if new metadata or a corrected source later becomes available—should it automatically update the record, or keep the migration flag until someone reviews it?

It should not automatically overwrite the record just because new metadata appears. I’d want it to mark the record as having new evidence or a pending update, keep the migration flag until someone reviews it, and then let a moderator decide whether to accept the correction. That way we preserve the audit trail and avoid silently changing older records.

When a record is flagged as a serious migration inconsistency, what should make it visible to staff or prioritized ahead of other review work—for example, severity, impact on search or linked records, or the type of asset involved?

Yes, severity should matter most, especially if the inconsistency affects identifiers, authorship, or anything that would mislead search results. Impact on linked records should also raise priority, because one bad migration there can affect several publications or author profiles at once. The type of asset matters too, with full-text items and highly cited or institutional records usually needing faster attention than a minor metadata-only entry.

When a migrated field comes from a questionable source, what practical rules should determine how far the traceability goes—for example, whether the system records the original file, import batch, or specific source record, and whether that trace should remain attached if the field is later corrected or replaced?

I’d want traceability at least back to the specific source record and the import batch, and for critical fields also to the original file if we have it. If the field is later corrected or replaced, the old trace should not disappear; it should stay in the history so we can see where the original value came from and why it changed. That audit trail is important for trust and for troubleshooting migration issues later.
What bulk import file formats should the system accept, and how should records in each format be mapped to the publication fields?

We’d definitely need support for the common library and repository formats, especially CSV, RIS, BibTeX, and ideally XML-based imports if they’re coming from another system. The mapping should be configurable so fields can be matched to our publication schema, because different sources label the same thing differently, and we don’t want to hardcode one import structure. If a file has extra fields, they should be preserved if possible or at least logged for review rather than dropped silently.

For those supported import formats, what operational rules should govern how the system handles records that don’t map cleanly to your publication schema, such as missing mandatory fields, duplicate entries, or ambiguous field values during import?

If a record is missing mandatory fields, I’d prefer it to be rejected from the main import but kept in an error report or staging area so someone can fix it and reimport it. For duplicates, the system should not blindly create a second record; it should either link to the existing one or flag it for review depending on how strong the match is. Ambiguous values should be imported as uncertain only if they can be clearly marked, otherwise they need to stay in a manual review queue.

When you accept XML-based imports from other systems, what practical rules should determine which XML structures or source variations are supported for mapping into your publication schema, and which ones should be rejected or held for manual review?

We’d support the XML structures that we can map reliably to our core publication fields, even if the source system uses different element names or nesting, as long as the meaning is clear. If the XML is too inconsistent, missing key metadata, or mixes several record types in a way that makes automatic mapping risky, then it should be rejected or sent to manual review. I’d also want us to prefer stable, documented source variants over ad hoc XML because otherwise the import rules become too fragile.

When an XML import is rejected or routed to manual review, what specific checks or thresholds should determine that decision, and are there any source-system patterns or record combinations that should be treated as acceptable exceptions?

The main threshold should be whether the system can map the mandatory fields with enough confidence to create a usable publication record. If title, at least one author or corporate creator, and some kind of date or identifier can’t be resolved, I’d route it to manual review rather than accept it automatically. Acceptable exceptions would be well-known source-system variants that we’ve already approved and tested, even if they use different tags or ordering, as long as the meaning is consistent.

When a source record contains mixed publication types or a combination of publication and non-publication metadata, what practical rule should determine whether it is split, mapped as one record, or sent to manual review?

If the mixed content clearly belongs to one publication, I’d map it as one record and keep the extra non-publication metadata only if it’s useful and doesn’t distort the bibliographic data. If the record actually contains multiple distinct publications or the publication part can’t be separated cleanly from the rest, it should be split only when the system can do that safely; otherwise it should go to manual review. The key rule is whether automatic handling would risk creating a wrong or misleading publication entry.

Beyond manual entry and citation-first external reconciliation, are there any other business events or source conditions that should trigger creation of a new publication record, such as staged imports from a bulk exchange, harvested metadata, or deposit workflows?

Yes, definitely. A new publication record should also be created when a staged bulk import has passed validation, when harvested metadata comes in from a trusted external feed and no matching record exists, and when a deposit workflow is completed by an author or administrator. For us, the rule is basically that if the source is considered authoritative enough and there isn’t already a reliable existing record, the system should create one rather than forcing users to re-enter it.

When you say the import mapping should be configurable, what are the specific expectations for schema and namespace handling in XML-based exchanges—for example, should the system adapt to source-specific namespaces automatically, require an explicit mapping template, or reject files whose schema can’t be matched cleanly?

I’d expect the system to support source-specific namespaces, but not by guessing. There should be an explicit mapping template or profile for each approved source schema, and the import should use that to translate the XML into our publication fields. If the namespace or schema doesn’t match a known template cleanly, it should be rejected or held for review rather than trying to infer the structure automatically.

Are there any source schemas or XML variants that should be accepted even if they are only partially documented, or do you want the import limited strictly to fully documented and approved source definitions?

We can be a bit flexible, but only in a controlled way. If a partially documented source has already been tested and we know the tag meanings well enough to map it safely, I’d accept it provisionally, with manual review for the uncertain parts. Anything completely unknown or too vague should wait until it’s properly documented and approved.

What rule should we use for author name variants when different spellings or forms appear—should the system treat them as the same author automatically, or only merge them when there is an approved authority record or manual confirmation?

It should not merge name variants automatically just because they look similar. We’d want an approved authority record, or at least a manual confirmation step, before treating different spellings or forms as the same author. Otherwise we risk collapsing distinct people, especially with common names or transliterated forms.

When a duplicate record can’t be confidently resolved, what specific conditions should trigger escalation to a more experienced reviewer versus leaving it in the review queue, and are there any cases where conflicting identifiers or publication-risk concerns would still be handled at the lower level?

If the duplicate affects a record that is already published, widely cited, or linked to reporting, I’d escalate it sooner, especially when conflicting identifiers point to different authors or institutions. Simple uncertainty in a new or low-impact record can stay in the normal review queue, as long as the reviewer can leave it untouched and move on. Only cases with clear publication-risk, like a possible merge that could corrupt the official bibliographic record, should go to the more experienced reviewer immediately.

Are there any language or localization expectations for the search, correction, and moderation screens—for example, specific languages, terminology, date or name formatting, or handling of mixed-language records—that the system needs to support?

Yes, the main expectation is that the interface should support at least English and French, since those are the practical working languages for us. For records themselves, we don’t want the system to force one language; mixed-language titles and abstracts should be preserved as entered, and formatting should follow the source where relevant, like names and dates in the bibliographic standard rather than a local display rewrite. If there are terminology choices on the screens, those should be consistent and clear, but I’d need to check whether Dutch is also required for some user groups.

For users who need a different interface language, what should happen when their preferred language is not available—should the system fall back to English, hide those language-specific options, or handle that some other way?

It should fall back to English by default. I wouldn’t want options to disappear unexpectedly, because that can make the interface feel broken; it’s better if the user still sees the full system with English labels where a translation is missing. If a screen has only partial translation, that’s acceptable as long as the core workflow still works consistently.

When the same term can be rendered differently across English, French, or any other supported language, do you want the system to enforce a single approved translation for screen labels and menus, or is it acceptable for terminology to vary as long as it remains clear and consistent within each language?

It’s better to have a single approved translation per language for labels and menus, so users don’t see different terms for the same action in different parts of the system. The wording can differ between English and French, of course, but within each language it should stay consistent. If a term is ambiguous, I’d prefer we standardize it early rather than letting each screen choose its own phrasing.

For the interface languages, are there any additional rules we should apply around translation coverage or fallback behavior—such as which screens must always be translated in English and French, and whether Dutch should appear automatically for any specific user groups or only where it is explicitly supported?

The critical screens, like search, upload, correction, and moderation, should always be available in English and French. Dutch should not appear automatically unless we explicitly decide to support it for a user group or a specific module; I’d rather not imply support we can’t maintain consistently. For less critical screens, partial translation is acceptable, but the main workflows need to be fully usable in the supported languages.
When two records may refer to the same person or organization, what rules should the system use to decide whether to normalize names, keep the source form, or treat them as separate entities?

The system should keep the source form in the record, but also normalize it into a standard authority form when we have a confirmed match. If there isn’t enough confidence, it should keep them separate and flag them for review rather than forcing a normalization. For organizations, I’d apply the same principle, especially when abbreviations or language variants could refer to different entities.

When a name or organization is not a confirmed exact match but looks similar, what operational rule should the system use to decide whether to auto-link it to an authority form, leave it unnormalized, or route it for manual review?

If it’s only a similar-looking match, the system should not auto-link it unless the confidence is high enough and the matching rules are very clear. Otherwise it should stay unnormalized and go to manual review, because a wrong authority link is harder to fix later than leaving it pending. I’d use auto-linking only for cases we’ve already agreed are safe, like exact variants or well-known standardized abbreviations.

When the system encounters a similar-name match in bibliographic extraction, what concrete rules should it use to decide whether the match is safe enough to auto-link versus requiring manual review, especially where abbreviations, transliterations, or other partial variants are involved?

For bibliographic extraction, auto-linking should be limited to cases where the match is essentially deterministic, like an exact normalized variant, a known abbreviation that we’ve already approved, or a transliteration that maps unambiguously to one authority form. If there is any real ambiguity, especially with common abbreviations or names that could belong to more than one person or institution, it should go to manual review. I’d rather the system be conservative there, because extraction errors can spread quickly through the publications data.

For migrating existing publication records and documents, what file formats should the bulk import process accept beyond CSV, RIS, BibTeX, and XML, and are there any format-specific rules for handling missing fields, mixed encodings, or embedded document attachments during import?

I don’t know if we want to commit to additional formats beyond those yet; I’d need to check what the current data sources actually are. For the known formats, missing fields should be allowed as long as the record is still usable, and the import should flag what couldn’t be mapped instead of failing the whole batch. Mixed encodings and embedded attachments should be handled carefully, but if they cause problems I’d prefer the import to quarantine those items for review rather than silently dropping data.

For items that are quarantined during import because of mixed encodings or embedded attachments, what should the review process do to resolve them—should staff correct the record and re-import it, extract the attachment separately, or leave the item out entirely if it can’t be safely mapped?

The review process should let staff correct the record and then re-import it, because we still want to preserve as much of the original publication data as possible. If there’s an embedded attachment, it should be extracted separately when feasible and linked back to the record. Only if it can’t be safely mapped or fixed should the item be left out, and that should be an explicit decision rather than an automatic drop.

Given the need to prioritize repository capabilities, what are the main business scenarios you care about most right now, and what outcomes should the repository support first in your day-to-day work?

The main thing is that researchers and library staff can reliably deposit publications and find the right records again later, including the full text where we have it. Day to day, we need fast search, safe upload and correction, and a moderation flow so questionable metadata can be checked before it becomes official. Bulk import and authority handling are also important, but I’d prioritize the core repository workflow first so people can actually use the system from end to end.
Are there any nice-to-have repository capabilities you’d want to defer to later phases, such as reporting, alerts, or integrations, and if so, what should determine when they become worth adding?

Yes, things like reporting dashboards, alerts, and integrations would be nice to have later, but they aren’t the first priority. I’d add them once the core deposit, search, correction, and moderation workflow is stable and we can see a clear operational need, like repeated manual work or regular requests from management. The deciding factor should be whether the feature saves time or improves data quality enough to justify the extra complexity.

When staff or researchers are searching and cannot find the right publication record right away, what should happen in the repository—should they be able to refine the search, browse related records, or fall back to another lookup path, and are there any cases where access or record status should prevent a result from being shown?

They should definitely be able to refine the search and browse related records, because that’s usually how people find the right publication when the first query is too broad or incomplete. If that still fails, a fallback lookup path like alternate author names, institution variants, or identifiers would be useful. Access or record status should limit what is shown if the publication is restricted or still under review, but the system should still indicate that a record exists when the user is allowed to know that.
